title: What are the rules for this() and super() in constructors?
shortTitle: What are the rules for this() and super() in constructors?
keyPoints: this() calls another constructor in the SAME class – used for constructor chaining
super() calls the PARENT class constructor – ensures parent is initialized first
this() or super() must be the FIRST statement in the constructor – you cannot have both
If you write neither, the compiler inserts super() (no-arg) automatically
If the parent has no no-arg constructor, you MUST explicitly call super(args) or the code does not compile
Construction order: parent first (super), then child – fields and init blocks run between super() and the rest of the constructor body

s1_definition.oneliner: this() delegates to another constructor in the same class. super() calls the parent constructor. One of them must be the first statement, and if you write neither, super() is inserted automatically.
s1_definition.profdef:
Constructor delegation rules:

- **this(args)** calls another constructor in the same class. Used to avoid duplicating initialization logic.
- **super(args)** calls a parent class constructor. Ensures the parent is fully initialized before the child.
- **Must be the first statement.** You cannot put any code before this() or super(), and you cannot use both in the same constructor.
- **Implicit super().** If you write neither this() nor super(), the compiler inserts `super()` (no-arg) automatically.
s1_definition.analogy: When opening a new bank branch (child class), the head office (parent class) must be set up first (super()). You can also delegate within the branch: the full-service opening procedure (one constructor) can delegate to a basic setup procedure (this()) to reuse common steps. But the very first thing that happens must be either calling head office or calling the basic setup.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  new SavingsAccount("SAV2001")
    │
    ▼
  SavingsAccount(String id)
    │ super(id) ← must be first
    ▼
  Account(String id)
    │ super() ← implicit call to Object()
    ▼
  Object() runs
    ▼
  Account field initializers + init blocks
    ▼
  Account constructor body
    ▼
  SavingsAccount field initializers + init blocks
    ▼
  SavingsAccount constructor body
    ▼
  Object fully constructed

  Rules:
    this() or super() must be FIRST statement
    Cannot use both in one constructor
    If neither written → implicit super()
    Parent no-arg missing + no explicit super(args) → COMPILE ERROR
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
this() delegates to another constructor in the same class, and super() calls the parent constructor. One of them must be the first statement in every constructor. If you write neither, the compiler inserts super() automatically.

The construction order is always parent first: super() runs, then the parent's field initializers and init blocks, then the parent's constructor body, then the child's field initializers and init blocks, then the child's constructor body.

If the parent class has no no-arg constructor, you must explicitly call super(args) or the code does not compile. Use this() chaining to avoid duplicating initialization logic across multiple constructors.

One sentence to remember: this() or super() must be the first statement, if neither is written super() is implicit, and the parent is always constructed before the child.
